content: Triple X syndrome, also referred to as trisomy X, triplo-X, XXX syndrome, or 47,XXX aneuploidy, is a chromosomal condition in which a human female has an additional X chromosome in each of her cells. This condition arises during the division of a parent’s reproductive cells and occurs approximately once in every 1,000 female births. Individuals with trisomy X typically do not exhibit any noticeable symptoms and are indistinguishable from females with a normal XX karyotype unless karyotyping is performed. Triple X syndrome is not inherited but rather results from a random event during the formation of reproductive cells (ova or sperm). An error in cell division, known as nondisjunction, can lead to reproductive cells with an extra chromosome. For instance, an oocyte or sperm cell may acquire an additional X chromosome due to nondisjunction. If such a cell contributes to the genetic makeup of a child, the child will have an extra X chromosome in all her cells. In some cases, trisomy X arises during cell division in early embryonic development. Some females with triple X syndrome have the extra X chromosome in only a subset of their cells, a condition referred to as 46,XX/47,XXX mosaicism. Due to the inactivation of one X chromosome and the formation of a Barr body in all female cells, only one X chromosome is active at any given time in a female cell. As a result, triple X syndrome generally does not cause unusual physical features or significant medical problems. Females with this condition are often taller than average, and their weight may be relatively low compared to their height. They may experience menstrual irregularities and, although severe mental impairments are rare, they have an increased risk of learning disabilities, delayed speech, and language development. A similar range of body types and characteristics is observed in both triple X syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome, including a lanky or youthful appearance, non-affectedness, or varying degrees of androgyny. The additional X chromosome can originate from either the maternal or paternal side. While body types and characteristics may be distinguishable in triple X syndrome, the condition is confirmed only through karyotype testing. Most women with triple X syndrome have normal sexual development and are capable of conceiving children. A small number may experience early onset of menstruation. Women with triple X syndrome are rarely diagnosed unless prenatal testing methods, such as amniocentesis, are performed. Most medical professionals do not consider the condition a disability. However, parents may seek such a designation to access early intervention treatments if mild developmental delays are present. Triple X syndrome occurs in approximately 1 in 1,000 female births. On average, five to ten girls with triple X syndrome are born in the United States each day. The first documented case of a woman with a 47,XXX karyotype was reported by Patricia A. Jacobs and colleagues at Western General Hospital in Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1959. The subject was a 35-year-old woman who was 5 feet 9 inches (176 cm) tall and weighed 128 pounds (58 kg). She experienced premature ovarian failure at the age of 19. At the time of her conception, her mother was 41 years old, and her father was 40.
